explanations.explanation: Close, but it flips the verse, friend. Solomon, David's son and Israel's king (Proverbs 1:1), says whoever is led astray by wine and strong drink “…is not wise.” He calls wine a mocker and strong drink a brawler, and nobody hands out gold stars for following those two. Wisdom is the one thing the verse says that person is missing.

That's right, friend. Solomon, David's son and Israel's king (Proverbs 1:1), says whoever is led astray by wine and strong drink “…is not wise.” Wine is called a mocker and strong drink a brawler. Anyone led astray by them is not wise.

That's what the verse says: whoever provokes the king forfeits his own life. The king's terror is compared to a lion's roar, so this isn't a small thing to stir up. Poking a lion is just not a plan, friend.
I wish that were the ending, friend, but the verse goes the other way. Whoever provokes the king forfeits his own life. A lion's roar doesn't usually end in a handshake.

explanations.answer: He gets a seat at court
explanations.explanation: No prize for this guy, friend. The verse says whoever provokes the king forfeits his own life. The king's terror is like a lion's roar, and nobody tugs on a lion's mane and walks away happy.
Yes, honorable. Solomon says it is honorable for a man to resolve a dispute. Then he adds that any fool will quarrel, which is the easy road. Ending an argument takes more strength than starting one.

Not pointless, friend. Solomon says it is honorable for a man to resolve a dispute. The one who is never short on arguments is the fool, since any fool will quarrel. Settling things is the part with honor in it.

I see why you'd think that, since arguments can get hot. But the verse calls resolving a dispute honorable. Dangerous isn't the word Solomon picks. He saves the harsh word for the fool who will quarrel.
That's it. At harvest time he looks, but nothing is there. He skipped the plowing in season, so he has nothing to gather. Seeds don't plant themselves, friend.
Plenty would be nice, friend, but the slacker didn't plow in season. So at harvest time he looks, but nothing is there. That's a long way from plenty.

Even a little is too generous here. The verse says the slacker does not plow in season, and at harvest time he looks, but nothing is there. Nothing, friend, not even a little. A little would be a pretty good day for him.

Yes, a man of understanding draws them out. The intentions of a man's heart are deep waters, and the verse says it's the man of understanding who draws them out. Deep water, friend, and he's the one who gets the bucket all the way down.
Money can buy a lot, friend, but not this. The verse says a man of understanding draws out the intentions of the heart. Deep waters need a wise person, and a fat wallet doesn't make you one.

You'd think a talker would get there first, but no. Solomon says a man of understanding draws the heart's intentions out. Lots of talking can just stir up the water. Understanding is what pulls the right things up.
Yes, a trustworthy man. Many a man proclaims his loving devotion, but who can find a trustworthy one? Words are cheap, friend. A trustworthy man is the rare one.
Wealth isn't what Solomon is hunting for. He asks who can find a trustworthy man. Plenty of men proclaim their loving devotion, and the question is who is actually dependable.
Strong is useful, friend, especially on moving day. But Solomon asks, “…who can find a trustworthy man?” He's looking past the big announcements for someone you can count on.
True. The righteous man walks with integrity, and the verse says blessed are his children after him. How he lives reaches past himself. His kids are in on the blessing.
It's actually true, friend. The proverb says the righteous man walks with integrity, and then it says blessed are his children after him. A life of integrity doesn't stop with him.

explanations.answer: No one can truly say it
explanations.explanation: Yes, that's where the question points. Solomon asks who can say, “I have kept my heart pure; I am cleansed from my sin…” and he doesn't name a single volunteer. The question just hangs there while nobody steps forward. I think that's his point.

Even kings don't get a pass here, friend. Solomon asks who can say, “I have kept my heart pure; I am cleansed from my sin…” and he doesn't name anybody. The verse before it has a king sifting out evil with his eyes, but that's about judging, not about claiming a clean heart.

explanations.answer: Any wise man can say it
explanations.explanation: Nice try, but he doesn't hand it to the wise either. Solomon asks who can say, “I have kept my heart pure; I am cleansed from my sin…” and the question points to no one. I think his point is that no one can truly say it, not even the wise.
That's the word. Differing weights and unequal measures are both detestable to the LORD. Cheating on the scale isn't a tiny thing to Him. He cares about honest dealing.

Not pleasing, friend. The verse says differing weights and unequal measures are both detestable to the LORD. The writer says it again later: "Unequal weights are detestable to the LORD, and dishonest scales are no good." (Proverbs 20:23) Twice in one chapter, so it's worth hearing.
Oh, it matters. Differing weights and unequal measures are both detestable to the LORD. Unimportant is the opposite of what the verse says. Honest scales are no small thing to Him.
Yes, actions. Even a young man is known by his actions, by whether his conduct is pure and upright. You can see who someone is by what they do. Age doesn't change that.
Words are easy to hand out, friend. The verse says even a young man is known by his actions, whether his conduct is pure and upright. What he does tells the story.

Friends can say something about a person, but that's not what this verse says. Even a young man is known by his actions, whether his conduct is pure and upright. It's his own conduct that shows who he is.
That's it. Do not love sleep, or you will grow poor. Then the verse says open your eyes, and you will have plenty of food. A pillow is a lovely thing, but it won't pay the bills.
Not wisdom, friend. This verse says do not love sleep, or you will grow poor. Loving sleep is the warning here, and wisdom isn't what the verse warns about.
Counsel is on the good side of the ledger, friend. A little later in this same passage, Solomon says to set plans by consultation. Here the warning is, do not love sleep, or you will grow poor.
Yes, he gloats. The buyer says “Worthless, worthless!” and then on the way out, he gloats. Sounds like the goods weren't so worthless after all. I think he likes his deal a little too much.
He already said his piece, friend. That's the “Worthless, worthless!” part. On the way out, the verse says he gloats, which is something else.
No apology on this walk out, friend. After calling the goods worthless, the buyer gloats on his way out the door. Sorry isn't in his vocabulary.
True. There is an abundance of gold and rubies, but lips of knowledge are a rare treasure. Gold and rubies come in abundance in this verse. Lips of knowledge are the rare treasure.
It's true, friend. Solomon says there is an abundance of gold and rubies, but lips of knowledge are a rare treasure. He's saying knowledge is the rarer find, even next to rubies.
That's the word. Food gained by fraud is sweet to a man, but later his mouth is full of gravel. The sweetness doesn't last, and the crunch comes after. Ouch, friend, my teeth hurt just reading it.

Honey is a sweet guess, friend, but the verse never mentions it. It says food gained by fraud is sweet to a man, but later his mouth is full of gravel. The sweetness comes first and the gravel comes later.
Bread would be a nice ending, but the verse isn't that kind. Food gained by fraud is sweet to a man, but later his mouth is full of gravel. That's the part that bites back.
Yes, by consultation. Solomon says to set plans by consultation, which means asking others and not just going it alone. Plans get better when more than one head is in the kitchen.
Secret planning isn't what the verse says. Solomon says to set plans by consultation. That means talking things over and not going it alone.
Lots aren't mentioned in this verse. Solomon says to set plans by consultation, and to wage war under sound guidance. He points to talking it through with others.

True. Right alongside setting plans by consultation, Solomon says to wage war under sound guidance. Both lines sit together in the same verse. Even the biggest, riskiest plans need good counsel behind them.
It's true, friend. The same verse says to set plans by consultation and to wage war under sound guidance. Big plans, same advice: get good guidance.

Yes, avoid. The verse says he who reveals secrets is a constant gossip, so avoid the one who babbles with his lips. If someone can't keep a secret, they're not the one to hand yours to. Simple enough to remember, friend.
Fixing people is tempting, friend, but that's not what the verse says. Solomon says to avoid the one who babbles with his lips. He's called a constant gossip, and the advice is to steer clear.
Please don't follow this one, friend. The verse says to avoid the one who babbles with his lips. He reveals secrets, and the instruction is to keep your distance.

explanations.answer: It goes out in deepest darkness
explanations.explanation: That's what the verse says. Whoever curses his father or mother, his lamp will be extinguished in deepest darkness. It's a heavy one, so I'm saying it plainly. Honoring parents matters.

explanations.answer: It passes on to his children
explanations.explanation: That isn't what the verse says, friend. It says his lamp will be extinguished in deepest darkness. It's a heavy word about whoever curses his father or mother.
The king isn't part of this one, friend. The verse says the lamp of whoever curses his father or mother will be extinguished in deepest darkness. It's a serious line.
Careful, friend, it's the other way around. Solomon says an inheritance gained quickly will not be blessed in the end. Fast money isn't a guarantee of lasting blessing.

That's right, friend. Solomon says an inheritance gained quickly will not be blessed in the end. The verse points to no blessing at the end, so getting it fast doesn't come out well. Quick isn't the same as blessed.
Yes, wait on the LORD. Solomon says not to say, “I will avenge this evil!” and tells us to wait on the LORD, and He will save you. Handing it to Him is the way out.
The king is all over this chapter, but not in this verse. Solomon says to wait on the LORD, and He will save you. That's where he points.
The verse doesn't ask you to forget a thing, friend. It says don't say you'll avenge it, and instead wait on the LORD, and He will save you. You hand it to Him and don't take it into your own hands.
True. Solomon says unequal weights are detestable to the LORD, and dishonest scales are no good. Weights came up earlier, in Proverbs 20:10. He's coming back to the same point, so I think it matters.
It's true, friend. Solomon says unequal weights are detestable to the LORD, and dishonest scales are no good. He's repeating himself on purpose, I think.
Close, friend, but it's the opposite. Solomon says a man's steps are from the LORD, so how can anyone understand his own way? That's a question, and it leans toward no. Nobody has it all figured out.

That's right. Solomon says a man's steps are from the LORD, and then asks how anyone can understand his own way. The question leans toward no. Our steps come from the LORD, and that's more than we can map out ourselves.

explanations.answer: Dedicating something rashly and reconsidering later
explanations.explanation: Yes. It is a trap for a man to dedicate something rashly, only later to reconsider his vows. The trap is the rash dedicating and the reconsidering that comes after. Think first, promise second.

explanations.answer: Making a vow out loud before others
explanations.explanation: The trap isn't saying it out loud, friend. The verse says it's a trap to dedicate something rashly, only later to reconsider his vows. Rashly is the key word.

explanations.answer: Waiting too long before making a vow
explanations.explanation: Waiting isn't the problem in this verse. The trap is to dedicate something rashly, only later to reconsider his vows. Rushing is what gets him.

explanations.answer: It searches out his inmost being
explanations.explanation: That's it. The spirit of a man is the lamp of the LORD, searching out his inmost being. It's a light that looks deep inside. The lamp belongs to the LORD, and it's the spirit of a man.

explanations.answer: It lights the path of the king
explanations.explanation: A king is nowhere in this verse, friend. It says the spirit of a man is the lamp of the LORD, searching out his inmost being. The lamp looks inward.

explanations.answer: It guards his house at night
explanations.explanation: A lamp that guards the house is a fun picture, but that's not what the verse says. The spirit of a man is the lamp of the LORD, searching out his inmost being. It looks deep inside.
Yes, loving devotion and faithfulness preserve a king, and by these he maintains his throne. Those are the two Solomon names. Character is what holds the throne in this verse.
Courage and wealth sound kingly, friend, but they're not on Solomon's list. The verse says loving devotion and faithfulness preserve a king. By these he maintains his throne.
Gold and soldiers look impressive, but Solomon doesn't pick them. He says loving devotion and faithfulness preserve a king, and by these he maintains his throne. Those are the two he names.
Yes, strength. The glory of young men is their strength. That's the first half of the saying. The second half is about the old.
Yes, gray. Gray hair is the splendor of the old. Those silver strands are called splendor here, friend, not something to hide. That's the second half of the saying.
Speed is a good guess, friend, but the verse says the glory of young men is their strength. Speed isn't mentioned. Strength is the word Solomon uses.
Long hair is a style choice, friend, but the verse says gray hair is the splendor of the old. Long isn't the word Solomon uses. That's what he calls their splendor: gray.
Dark hair is lovely, but Solomon says gray hair is the splendor of the old. Dark isn't the word in this verse. It's the gray that gets the honor.
Yes, cleanse. Solomon says lashes and wounds scour evil, and beatings cleanse the inmost parts. This is a heavy one, so I'll just stick to what the verse says. The word it uses is cleanse.
Harden isn't the word, friend. Solomon says lashes and wounds scour evil, and beatings cleanse the inmost parts. It's a heavy verse, so I'll keep to the plain wording.
The verse doesn't say weaken, friend. It says lashes and wounds scour evil, and beatings cleanse the inmost parts. It's a heavy one, so I'll leave it plain.
